why_angle: The cited pages agree on 24 A. For 3-prong outlets they only say 'needs an electrician' or 'special caution'. None of them quotes NEC 250.140, whose permission to use the neutral as the ground on an existing 3-wire circuit names only ranges, ovens, cooking units and dryers, not EV chargers. None names the NEC 625.54 GFCI requirement either. This page applies that rule to each charger's plug in the table, alongside maker-store prices checked 2026-11-17 that are $40 to $50 below the Amazon prices the rival pages quote.

page.after:
What the differences mean

On a 30 A dryer circuit, every charger above charges at the same speed: 24 A × 240 V = 5.76 kW. In a home supplied at 208 V it is 24 A × 208 V = 4.99 kW, about 13% less.

  • An average day of driving: 13,735 mi a year (FHWA) ÷ 365 = 37.6 mi. A 2026 Model Y Long Range AWD uses 27 kWh/100 mi (EPA, measured at the wall), so that day takes 37.6 × 0.27 = 10.2 kWh. At 24 A that is 10.2 ÷ 5.76 = 1.8 hours on the charger.
  • A full 10-hour night: 10 × 5.76 = 57.6 kWh, and 57.6 ÷ 0.27 = 213 miles of range.
  • Cost: 10.2 kWh × 18.16 ¢ (EIA US residential average, August 2026) = $1.84 a day.
  • Price per kW you can actually use on a dryer circuit: EVDANCE 14-30 at $229.95 ÷ 5.76 = $39.92/kW. Grizzl-E Mini at $349.99 ÷ 5.76 = $60.76/kW. The 40 A Grizzl-E charges no faster on this outlet.

3-prong or 4-prong: what the electrical code allows

A 4-prong NEMA 14-30 has two hots, a neutral and a separate ground. An older 3-prong NEMA 10-30 has two hots and a neutral, with no ground. NEC 250.140, titled "Frames of Ranges and Clothes Dryers", covers "frames of electric ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers, and outlet or junction boxes". Its rule (A) says the circuit "shall include an equipment grounding conductor". The exception in (B) applies "for existing branch-circuit installations only": it lets those listed appliances use the neutral as their ground. An EV charger is not on that list. So a charger plugged into a 10-30 has no ground the code allows, even though the dryer before it did.

Each charger on a 4-prong outlet holds 24 A in a different way. Both EVDANCE 14-30 models top out at 24 A, so no setting can overload a 30 A circuit. Tesla's 14-30 and 10-30 adapters "automatically reduce your charge rate to 24 Amps", according to NeoCharge. NeoCharge also warns that a generic NEMA adapter lets the Mobile Connector draw 32 A, which can trip a 30 A breaker. The Grizzl-E Mini ships set to 40 A, and Plug & Range notes it "can not detect the circuit amperage limit". Its cap is a DIP switch behind the front cover, so you have to set it before the first charge.

Ground-fault protection: NEC 625.54 calls for GFCI protection on receptacles installed for EV charging equipment. EC&M reports that a 2026 amendment (TIA 1892), written because a charger's own ground-fault circuit and a GFCI breaker can trip each other, passed its ballot on May 29, 2026. EVDANCE publishes no leakage-trip figure, so ask your electrician whether the dryer breaker needs to be a GFCI and test a full night's charge.

Not recommended

EVDANCE NEMA 10-30 models on a 3-wire outlet. They fit the old 3-prong socket, but with no ground on that circuit they rely on the exception 250.140(B) gives only to dryers and ranges. The 10-30 J1772 listing also describes a 40 A, 14-50 charger in its body text, so don't buy from its specs until EVDANCE fixes the page. Adapter stacks. A 14-30-to-14-50 pigtail on a charger or adapter made for a 14-50 makes the plug fit but doesn't lower the current the charger draws. J+ Booster 2. It costs $749 at J+ Americas, and the maker's adapter list includes no 14-30 or 10-30 adapter.
